author: Hamza Shaikh
content:
AI coding agents just got smarter—and accidentally leaked secrets into public GitHub repos.

Two major shifts just landed in the AI developer ecosystem:
→ Model Context Protocol (MCP) + Agent Skills joined forces under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) alongside JetBrains 2026.3 ("Air"), Gemini 4 Carbon, and Claude Fable 5.2.
→ Security researchers at Apiiro revealed how autonomous auto-mode runs caused coding agents to store local API tokens inside config files that developers accidentally pushed to public repos.

That exact failure mode is why I built AgentForge around deterministic permission tiers instead of "run anything" shell access:

1. `read` & `local-write` steps stay fast inside your workspace.
2. `external-write`, `publish`, & `destructive` steps pause cleanly at a human approval checkpoint.
3. Secrets stay isolated behind environment variables—never written into manifests or logs.

author: Ishu Mishra
content:
We need to talk about the hidden cost of AI in software development.

I recently noticed a mid-senior engineer (6+ YoE) struggling to debug a straightforward client-side issue. 

Instead of isolating the problem or using browser dev tools, the default reflex was: "Ask AI to fix it."

The scenario is genuinely concerning. When we skip the struggle of debugging, we lose the deep intuition that separates senior engineers from junior ones.

If you use AI daily, try this rule:

1. Reproduce the bug yourself.
2. Form a hypothesis on why it's breaking.
3. Use AI to validate your fix or explore edge cases—not as your first line of defense.

Stay sharp. Keep debugging.

author: John Crickett
content:
“AI will replace software engineers because it can write all the code.”

Nope.

Several years ago I built software that unlocked more than $10M a year in additional profit for the business.

The code took less than two weeks.

With today’s AI tools, I could probably do it in under a week. Maybe even a day.

But the code wasn’t the hard part.

The hard part took months:

Understanding a messy domain.
Pressure-testing assumptions with experts.
Working through edge cases.
Deciding what not to build.
Making tradeoffs around risk, complexity, and value, then getting stakeholders to sign off on them.

By the time I wrote most of the code, much of the real engineering had already happened.

That’s why “AI can write code, therefore AI can replace engineers” misses the point.

Code is an output of engineering.

AI makes that output faster and cheaper.

But someone still has to understand the problem, challenge the assumptions, make the tradeoffs, and decide what the software should actually do.

That’s the engineering.
